claims.text: OpenSecrets' series of contributions from pro-Israel PACs (PAC money only) runs from about $4.0M in 1990 to $2.1M in 2000, $5.1M in 2012, $5.9M in 2014, $7.5M in 2016, $8.7M in 2018 and $8.7M in 2020, a total of $71.3M for 1990–2020.

Cumulatively 1990–2020 the largest pro-Israel PACs were J Street PAC ($14.5M), NORPAC ($8.1M), National PAC ($4.5M), the Republican Jewish Coalition ($3.4M) and National Action Committee ($2.9M); J Street gave $4.2M in 2018 alone; Pro-Israel America PAC gave $905,889 and DMFI $337,135 in 2020.

The Washington Report on Middle East Affairs, from FEC data, reported pro-Israel PAC contributions to House and Senate candidates of $12,661,440 (2019–20), $17,175,455 (2021–22) and $44,656,374 (2023–24).

By the end of July 2024, per FEC data compiled by Sludge, AIPAC PAC had spent $44.8M ($42M to candidates, parties and leadership PACs, mostly earmarked individual donations) and UDP about $55.4M (more than $35M in independent expenditures), about $100.2M combined; AIPAC PAC had given Wesley Bell more than $3.1M.

The Guardian found pro-Israel donors had given over $58M to sitting members of Congress in their most recent elections, all but 33 members receiving some; the top six 2022 recipients, all centrist Democrats, received about $25M (about 42%); members supportive of Israel after 7 Oct 2023 averaged about $125,000 against about $18,000 for supporters of Palestinians; party, not money, predicted statements on civilian casualties.

Per FEC filings and OpenSecrets, 2022→2024 spending: AIPAC/UDP $44M→$95.1M; RJC and its super PAC $4.5M→$19.7M; J Street $8.6M→$14.6M; DMFI $7.7M→$4.8M; NORPAC $1.6M→$2.7M (fundraising events up from about 40 to 60 a year); Miriam Adelson gave the RJC super PAC $5M and was the largest individual donor to outside groups in 2024.

claims.text: Per OpenSecrets data analysed by the Guardian, pro-Israel donors and lobbyists spent more than $22M on lobbying and contributions in the 2018 cycle: about $5M on lobbying (the most since tracking began in 1998, AIPAC about $3.5M) and just under $15M in contributions (the most since 1990), to 269 House members and 57 senators, about two-to-one to Democrats.

The largest pro-Israel contributors in 2018 were J Street PAC ($4.03M), NorPAC ($1.1M) and the Republican Jewish Coalition (about $502,000); the top recipients were Sens. Bob Menendez ($548,507), Ted Cruz ($352,894), Sherrod Brown ($230,342), Tammy Baldwin ($229,896) and Senate candidate Beto O'Rourke ($226,690).

For comparison, in the 2018 cycle the securities and investment industry spent $389M and real estate $186M (Guardian, from OpenSecrets); the US-Cuba Democracy PAC gave about $171,000; FARA registrants working for Israeli principals reported about $46.3M in 2017–2018, about $2.1M of it for political activity and $44.2M for tourism and other industries.

Sludge reported that AIPAC has spent more than $3M a year on federal lobbying since 2014, that AIPAC's charity arm spent $15.7M on congressional visits to Israel since 2000 (LegiStorm), that Sheldon and Miriam Adelson spent $123M on the 2018 midterms, nearly all benefiting Republicans, and that Haim Saban gave $3.3M to Democratic outside groups in 2018.
Fairshake, the cryptocurrency industry's super PAC, and its affiliates spent over $133M in 2024 and had raised more than $193M for the 2026 midterms by January 2026.

claims.text: For the full 2023–2024 cycle Sludge counted nearly $126.9M in combined AIPAC PAC and UDP spending: more than $55.2M donated to federal candidates (at least $45.2M to members of the 119th Congress) and almost $61M disbursed by UDP, including about $37.9M in independent expenditures for House candidates and nearly $8.6M given to six other PACs.

AIPAC's PAC gave $45.9M to members of Congress, their caucus PACs and federal candidates in the 2026 cycle through 31 July 2026, overwhelmingly earmarked contributions from individuals, focused on members of the Defense and Appropriations committees.
